target.question: What relative and absolute chronology can be justified for the undated correspondence bundle?

mapping.state: What is acted on: the undated correspondence bundle, treated at two levels. (1) The bundle as a unit, whose custody history (creator, recipient, later holders, accession) is only partially known. (2) Each item in it (letter, envelope, enclosure, draft or copy), whose date of writing, posting and receipt is unknown. Counterpart of the source's 'dispersed records with dated traces': any trace, inside or outside the bundle, that may carry a date or an order relation. Candidate traces are postmarks and postage, letterhead, paper and watermark, handwriting, recipient dockets or endorsements, internal mentions of events, persons, addresses or weekday/date combinations, references from one letter to another, accession and custody records, and independent event records or calendars. Assumptions, not supplied facts: the packet does not say which of these traces exist for this bundle, whether envelopes belong to the letters they now accompany, whether the bundle is a single correspondence or a later assembly, or whether the present physical arrangement reflects original order. Each is treated as open until checked.
mapping.operation: Proposed procedure. (1) Record the bundle as found before moving anything: give each item an identifier and note its physical position, attachments, folds and enclosures. Physical arrangement is kept as a separate record from any proposed writing order. (2) For each item, enter every candidate dating trace in a register with its type: internal reference, material feature, inter-letter reference, or custody/annotation record. (3) Classify what each trace can bound: not-before (terminus post quem), not-after (terminus ante quem), or a relative link (item A precedes item B, for example B answers or cites A). Also record which event it dates: writing, posting, receipt, docketing or accession. (4) Record the origin of each trace and whether it could derive from another trace, for example a later docket copied from an envelope, or a catalogue date copied from a docket. Dependent traces count as one. (5) Cross-check traces against independent external records such as event records, calendars for weekday/date combinations, and accession or custody records. (6) Assemble the supported relative links into a partial order and the bounds into a date interval per item. Mark as explicit gaps every item with no usable trace and every interval not covered by any supported link. (7) Where a trace fits more than one placement, keep each alternative chronology rather than choosing one. (8) On contradiction, recheck in this order: transcription, item identification, envelope-to-letter association, which event the trace dates, and independence of the records. If the conflict persists, record it as unresolved; do not average or silently discard. Stopping condition: stop when every item either has a cited interval and/or order position or is explicitly marked unplaced, and when checking the remaining accessible records no longer changes any bound or order relation, or when accessible records are exhausted. Follow-up: for each gap or conflict, name the specific independent anchor that would resolve it (a counterpart letter held elsewhere, an event record, another dated reference document) and seek it. Re-run steps 5-8 when a new record is obtained.
mapping.signal: What can be observed once the register is assembled. (a) Compatible links: bounds from independent traces on the same item overlap, and inter-letter references yield an order with no cycles, consistent with those bounds. (b) Contradictions: non-overlapping intervals for one item, an order cycle (A before B before A), or a custody record that places the bundle somewhere incompatible with an item's bounds. (c) Missing intervals: items with no trace, items bounded on one side only, and stretches of the sequence joined by no supported link. (d) Dependence indicators: shared wording, shared errors or identical dates across records, suggesting one was copied from another. (e) Divergence between the physical arrangement and the trace-supported order. These are what the procedure would look for; the packet reports no such observations for this bundle.
mapping.inference: Compatible independent links warrant a bounded reconstruction, reported in three tiers. Established: a relative position or date interval supported by two or more independent, mutually compatible traces. Provisional: supported by a single trace or by traces whose independence is not shown. Unresolved: conflicting or absent support. Relative chronology is justified only as a partial order: items joined by supported links are ordered, the rest are left unordered relative to one another. Absolute chronology is justified only as intervals, each stated as not-before/not-after with its supporting traces and the event it dates. It narrows to a specific date only where an independent trace fixes one and the link between that trace and the item is itself supported. A custody or accession date can bound the bundle as a whole (items present at accession were written no later than it) only under the stated assumption that the bundle's contents at accession are those now present. It does not order items within the bundle. Physical arrangement is treated as a hypothesis about order, to be tested against traces, not as evidence of writing order. Where alternatives survive, the justified result is the set of alternative chronologies with their gaps marked.
mapping.limit: Source limits carried over with target counterparts. Records may be lost or inaccessible: counterpart letters, envelopes or accession files may not survive, so gaps may be permanent. Anonymous or ambiguous: unsigned letters, shared names, recurring events and reused addresses can attach a trace to the wrong person, event or year. Forged or mistaken: items may be backdated, misdated by the writer, or misdocketed by a recipient or later custodian. Copied from one another: dockets, catalogue entries and accession notes may repeat a single earlier guess, so agreement among them is not independent confirmation. Misassociation: an envelope may not belong to the letter it accompanies. A postmark dates posting, not writing. Paper, watermark or letterhead gives at most a not-before bound, since stock may be used long afterwards. Handwriting comparison supports only coarse placement. Absence is not evidence: no surviving reply does not establish that none was written, and no letters from an interval does not establish that correspondence stopped. A continuous-looking sequence can still contain misplaced or misidentified items or undocumented breaks. Transfer limits: provenance reconstruction follows one object through successive custody, whereas here many items are dated by creation and exchange, so custody links do not translate into writing order. The bundle may be a later assembly from several correspondences, in which case one chronology may not apply. This mapping is a scoped authored hypothesis, not verified practitioner consensus. Quantitative alignment of long measured sequences is not assumed to be customary practice and is not relied on here.

explanation.operational_chain: The mapping keeps the source's sequence of partial history, gathering and cross-checking records, compatible or conflicting links, bounded reconstruction, and limits. State identifies the bundle and its individual items as the things with partially known histories and lists the kinds of trace that could carry dates, flagging which are assumed and not supplied. Operation turns 'gather and cross-check' into a register of traces classified by the bound each can give and by independence, assembled into a partial order and per-item intervals, with gaps marked, a defined stopping point and named follow-ups. Signal specifies what agreement, contradiction, missing coverage and dependence would look like in that register. Inference restricts the conclusion to tiered, interval-based and partially ordered claims. Limit restates each source caveat in terms of letters, envelopes, dockets and custody records, and notes where the source and target differ.
explanation.why_source_structure_applies: Both tasks reconstruct a sequence from scattered, incomplete records, where each record gives only a partial constraint and where independence among records determines how much weight their agreement carries. The source's practice of arranging supported links and marking unsupported intervals as gaps matches the practitioner baseline of converging independent date clues, preserved uncertain intervals and retained alternative chronologies. Its warning that a continuous-looking chronology can hide misidentified transitions corresponds to the baseline's separation of physical arrangement from original order. The structure applies with an adjustment: the source tracks custody of one object, while the target dates the creation of many items, so custody records serve as bounds on the bundle and not as evidence of writing order.
explanation.uncertainty: The packet supplies no description of the bundle's actual contents, so which traces exist, how many items can be placed, and whether any absolute date can be fixed are unknown. The procedure is proposed, and no observations have been made. The assumptions that the bundle is a single correspondence, that envelopes belong to their letters, and that accession contents match present contents are unestablished and are stated as conditions in the mapping. The practitioner baseline is itself a scoped authored hypothesis, not verified consensus, so the fit between this procedure and ordinary archival practice is likewise provisional. The result may remain a partial order with wide intervals and permanent gaps.
